# Feature: GLM-5.3-Flash

## Goal

Run the immutable official GLM-5.3-Flash checkpoint with Krasis's normal
full-GPU prefill and Rust/CUDA hybrid decode path, without weakening existing
model support, calibration, correctness, or launcher capability gates.

## Pinned source

- Repository: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash`
- Revision: `3f1971b7b5f7a528c9c4ef6212c8785298a8c24a`
- License: MIT

The source contains 62 safetensors shards. The immutable checkpoint identity
must be computed by the unified checkpoint identity system after download.

## Measured architecture contract

- 45 main text layers plus a separate MTP block
- 34 Kimi Delta Attention layers and 11 DSA layers
- 3 dense MLP layers followed by 42 sparse MoE layers
- 288 routed experts, top-8, one shared expert
- 4-way mHC at both attention and MLP residual sites
- DSA uses 4-token learned k-pool compression, expands selected pools to raw
  indices, and retains the visible incomplete tail
- Source dense, attention, and expert tensors use checkpoint-declared 128x128
  FP8 block scales; no source-format guess or raw-FP8 fallback is permitted

## Implementation boundary

1. Parse and validate the model's explicit schedules and dimensions.
2. Load block-scaled FP8 tensors in both Python setup and Rust weight paths.
3. Implement KDA prefill/decode and persistent recurrent/conv state in
   Rust/CUDA, not Python.
4. Reuse generalized mHC math while preserving DeepSeek-V4's learned final
   head and GLM-5.3's unweighted final stream mean.
5. Extend DSA with the measured k-pool indexer contract without changing
   GLM-5.2 IndexShare semantics.
6. Add HQQ attention cache descriptors for KDA and DSA; production validation
   remains INT4 experts and measured HQQ attention only.
7. Expose only witness-validated text capability initially. Vision remains
   unsupported until it receives its own correctness and launcher gate.

## Acceptance

- Complete immutable download and checkpoint inventory verification.
- Synthetic config, source-dequant, CUDA recurrence, k-pool, mHC, and
  cross-model regression tests pass.
- Llama witness agrees at defined trace/logit/token checkpoints. HF output is
  not accepted as the correctness source.
- Real launcher-started A6000 service completes calibration, respects the
  runtime-measured 600 MiB margin, serves a real request, and has no budget,
  slot, copy, CUDA, or OOM errors.
- Speed is measured only after timing/trace instrumentation is disabled.

## Current state

Text mode is operational and the measurement-led prefill/decode campaign is
complete on the RTX A6000 and RTX PRO 6000. The immutable 62-shard checkpoint
and its checkpoint-qualified 157.5 GB Marlin/HQQ cache are complete. The exact
final timing-disabled RTX PRO benchmark reached 1,420.5 tok/s prefill at
39,920 tokens and 23.87 tok/s best internal decode. Startup measured every
500/4K/8K/16K/32K/39,920 VRAM probe, decode held 1,279 MiB free, and all HCS,
CUDA, and OOM failure counters remained zero.

The exact final server built a fresh identity-matched six-prompt heatmap and
passed `./dev network 18254 --large` `18/18`. Canonical real-content prompts
were coherent at 2,044/8,585/23,072 tokens; 61,891 tokens correctly rejected
above the test profile's 50,000-token cap; all five sequential memory turns
passed. The service was stopped normally after the gate and both local GPUs
are idle.

The final launcher contract recognizes only the pinned checkpoint revision and
offers HQQ6 attention, k6v6 KV, INT4 experts, one GPU, and the qualified 4,096
token context. Vision and multi-GPU execution remain unsupported and fail
closed. A combined GLM-5.3 llama-witness profile is not yet available, so this
is operational text acceptance rather than the feature's final witness/release
correctness gate.

## Initial decode performance profile

The initial accepted timing-disabled real-content result was 6.34 tok/s. This
was the first correctness-qualified baseline, before targeted optimization.
One timing-enabled diagnostic was used only for attribution.

Each token selects 42 sparse layers x top-8 experts = 336 routed experts. The
loaded Marlin cache measured 12.375 MiB per expert including scales, giving an
exact selected routed-expert footprint of 4,158 MiB/token (4,032 MiB for the
raw INT4 matrices). At 249 measured decode steps, Dynamic HCS hit 61.52% and
reduced physical expert DMA to 1,599.90 MiB/token. That transfer consumed
77.57 ms/token at 21.54 GB/s; graph events consumed another 48.57 ms/token,
for 135.70 ms/token total under timing instrumentation.

On the same A6000, accepted DeepSeek-V4 evidence measured 3,192.75 MiB/token
selected, 781.51 MiB/token physical DMA, 35.70 ms H2D, and 34.93 ms graph
events. GLM-5.3 therefore selects 30.2% more packed expert data, physically
moves 2.05x as much after HCS, and spends 39.0% more time in graph work. These
measurements explain the initial speed without assigning an unmeasured cause.
These measurements drove the first optimization pass below.

## First optimization pass

The original timing-disabled A6000 standard baseline was `67.6/86.2 tok/s`
prefill at 1K/3,196 tokens and `7.32/7.79/7.57 tok/s` decode at 50/100/250.
Instrumentation showed that KDA recurrence was only 2.15 ms/token, while Q/K/V
projection was 10.45 ms, post-HCS expert transfer dominated the MoE path, and
the long prefill left substantial work outside KDA recurrence. This ruled out
a recurrence-only rewrite.

The prefill root cause was an existing native-DSA gathered-attention capability
gate that also required `deepseek_v4_hc_mult == 0`. GLM-5.3 has valid registered
native DSA and mHC simultaneously, so it was incorrectly excluded. Capability
is now derived from the registered native-DSA descriptor and absence of the
separate DeepSeek-V4 descriptor; it contains no model name, GPU identity, or
fixed geometry. A CUDA parity test passed. Timing-disabled A6000 prefill then
reached as much as `84.2/169.2 tok/s`; the exact final cleaned run reproduced
`79.5/162.5`, bounding ordinary run variance.

The decode root cause was a global evictable-slot suffix paired with layer-local
victim selection. At high RTX PRO residency this produced 34 no-slot events
despite 6,600 total residents. The runtime now preserves the same calibrated
tail count but allocates it across all runtime-discovered active layers and
deterministically redistributes unused quota from short layers. It changes no
VRAM budget, resident count, model constant, or GPU constant. The paired A6000
run improved decode from `6.94/7.61/7.29` to `7.36/8.18/7.76 tok/s`
(`+6.0/+7.5/+6.4%`). The RTX PRO result was `20.74/22.26/21.61 tok/s`, with
all prior no-slot events eliminated. Both cards kept zero budget skips and copy
failures and stayed above the 600 MiB margin.

Final review made this policy fail closed: every loaded slot must occur exactly
once in the runtime layer map, capacity and target counts must agree, and the
tail must cover every active layer. The previous silent global-suffix fallback
was removed. The focused invariant suite passed `4/4`; the exact reviewed
timing-disabled repeats measured `79.1/162.1` prefill and
`6.83/7.67/7.29` decode on A6000, and `106.0/265.8` prefill and
`20.50/22.26/21.61` decode on RTX PRO, with zero budget, slot, copy, CUDA, or
OOM failures.

Same-host DeepSeek-V4 controls measured 101.5/167.9 tok/s at 1K prefill on
A6000/PRO and `12.96/13.51/12.94` / `37.20/38.17/36.63 tok/s` decode. GLM
therefore reached 83.0%/63.9% of 1K prefill and 56.8-60.5%/55.8-59.0% of
decode. The requested half-speed target is met on both cards; three-quarter
decode is not yet met.

Two tempting shortcuts were rejected from measured evidence. A fixed five-
block HCS tail helped A6000 but was not portable; the layer-balanced runtime
policy slightly exceeded it without changing tail size. Parallel Q/K/V CUDA
streams regressed A6000 decode by `4.1/3.1/3.0%` and prefill by `4.3/3.1%`, so
that entire candidate branch was removed. Global LRU improved only the long
shadow while regressing short requests, and every prompt-static blend was
worse; neither became a fallback or default.

The mandatory cross-model gate found and fixed one parser regression before
handoff: GLM's unified nested KDA head geometry had accidentally been applied
to Qwen3-Next. Family-specific parsing now preserves QCN's checkpoint-declared
16 key / 32 value heads and independent dimensions. The exact timing-disabled
`./dev speed-test` passed with best 2,598.6 tok/s prefill, 55.18 tok/s decode,
24,576/24,576 HCS residents, 4,204 MiB free, and zero failures.

The post-review exact repeat also passed: best prefill was 2,595.1 tok/s and
best internal decode was 54.40 tok/s, with the same complete HCS residency,
4,204 MiB floor, and clean failure counters.

## RTX PRO full long-context benchmark

A separate test-only 50,000-token profile was qualified without changing the
accepted 4K service profile. Runtime calibration stepped through 4K, 8K, 16K,
32K, and 39,920 tokens rather than assuming the checkpoint limit was safe. The
39,920-token probe held 1,199 MiB free against the unchanged 600 MiB runtime
margin, and the complete timing-disabled standard benchmark passed.

Internal prefill scaled from `114.8 tok/s` at 1K to `565.2 tok/s` at 35K and
remained flat at `564.6 tok/s` at 39,920. Internal decode was
`21.59/21.94/21.39 tok/s` at 50/100/250 target tokens. The fresh exact-runtime
heatmap retained 6,560/12,096 HCS experts; decode minimum free VRAM was
1,285 MiB. Every HCS failure counter remained zero and no CUDA error or OOM
occurred. The later exact-source operational gate additionally qualified real
canonical content through 23,072 tokens, but it does not replace long-context
llama-witness parity.

The subsequent campaign closed the measured prefill and decode frontier at the
requested 5% whole-model threshold. Further work would require a new measured
bottleneck or a materially different algorithm rather than another known
isolated candidate. Vision, multi-GPU, long-context llama-witness parity, and
the combined llama-witness profile remain explicitly unqualified.

## RTX PRO long-prefill bottleneck profile

The 35K/39,920 plateau was profiled separately from speed evidence, using CUDA
events and synchronization only for attribution. At 39,920 tokens, the named
stages closed to within 4.3 ms of a 68,756.7 ms total. KDA recurrence consumed
28,589.1 ms (41.6%), DSA attention 20,942.6 ms (30.5%), FFN 10,066.3 ms
(14.6%, including 6,069.4 ms of expert staging/DMA), and the two mHC prep/norm
stages 3,595.5 ms (5.2%). KDA convolution and QKV projection consumed another
4,369.7 ms. This makes the current recurrent KDA prefill implementation the
first measured target; expert staging is not the primary long-prompt limit.

The official KDA inference design uses chunkwise prompt processing, while the
current Krasis kernel launches only one block per head and iterates prompt
tokens inside that block. The portable implementation target is therefore a
native CUDA chunkwise KDA path with token-parallel chunk preparation and a
head-parallel state recurrence. It must support Ampere, derive geometry and
scratch from the loaded descriptor, and select tuning from measurement rather
than a model/GPU constant. The recurrent implementation remains useful as a
test oracle; unsupported production geometry must fail closed rather than
silently fall back.

A timing-disabled A/B of the existing bounded BF16-materialized HQQ projection
path improved the same 39,920-token calibration from approximately 562.6 to
591.6 tok/s (+4.9%) and held 1,207 MiB minimum free VRAM. It is a secondary
candidate after correctness validation, not a substitute for KDA/DSA work.
Next priorities are: chunkwise KDA; isolated DSA substage/materialization work;
the existing TF32 mHC projection A/B; only then FFN DMA/computation overlap.

## Second optimisation campaign and stopping decision
